transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Jamal Ortiz (Redwood SE), Lena Howard (CTO, Apogee), Raj Patel (Head of ML), Sofia Moreno (DevOps), Chris Neal (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): discuss quickstart credits/time-to-first-token; evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private; security + compliance questions; plan for bench-to-prod pilot.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thank you for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood inference, I'm the account exec on this account, with me is Jamal our systems SE. quick intro round?
[00:12] Lena: Hi I'm Lena, CTO at Apogee, we build a document understanding pipeline for enterprise clients, trying to figure out how to get from prototype to production, hi all.
[00:20] Raj: Raj, head of ML, running most of the model infra experiments.
[00:24] Sofia: Sofia, DevOps, I own infra and networking.
[00:28] Chris: Chris PM, running the vendor evaluation.
[00:31] Jamal: Jamal here, Redwood SE, I focus on inference perf and private deployments.
[00:35] Maya: Cool, we'll do a quick agenda: 1) understand your current stack and success criteria, 2) walk hosting options (hosted/dedicated/private), 3) quickstart credits/time-to-first-token and what the pilot looks like, 4) next steps. Sound good?

[01:00] Lena: Yes. For context: last year we built an internal prototype on open-source models, running in our kubernetes cluster and some experiments on SageMaker. Prototype is fine but cost and latency at scale are concerns. We need predictable per-request latency under 300ms p95 for short responses, and end-to-end throughput of around 120 qps for our busiest endpoints.

[01:35] Raj: Also data residency: some clients require that all documents stay in-region, and a few are sensitive PII. We need KMS-managed encryption and audit logs for access. SOC2 is a must for vendor selection.

[02:05] Maya: Great — that's typical. Jamal, can you talk through hosting tradeoffs quickly?

[02:12] Jamal: Sure. Broadly three lanes: hosted API is the fastest to get devs to first token — we can give you PLG credits, SDKs, streaming responses. Hosted is multi-tenant but we have strong tenant isolation and SOC2 controls. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput — you get higher throughput per dollar at scale and capacity guarantees. Private is a VPC or on-prem deployment where the control plane is customer-managed for data residency and extra compliance. Each has differences in integration and network setup.

[03:01] Raj: For the dedicated option — do we still get the same operator features? tracing, rollouts, and the console?

[03:10] Jamal: Yes, you get the Redwood Console with tracing hooks, token-level cost breakdowns, and rollout policies. For private, the control plane is customer-managed but we can enable a restricted console or an API-only control plane depending on your question. There is some additional setup for vpc peering and routing.

[03:36] Lena: Timeline wise: we want a pilot running in Jan, and a decision by end of Q1. We're hoping to prove with real data that latency and cost meet our KPI. How fast can we have engineers make the first call — time-to-first-token — and what do you usually provide?

[04:00] Maya: For PLG/self-serve we provision free credits (we can make 30k tokens or 30k units depending on embeddings vs generative - we'll tailor this). Developers can be up and making calls within a couple hours using our SDK or curl. For the pilot we usually provision larger credits and a small dedicated capacity if needed for consistent perf. Jamal, any notes on bench runs?

[04:33] Jamal: We'll run two types of bench: synthetic latency tests and a throughput/quality run with your dataset. For the latter we request a redacted sample dataset (10-20 documents or about 5-10k tokens) and an expected QPS profile. We'll run a perf script that exercises KV cache and prefix caching — those reduce cost for repeated contexts. Metric outputs: token latency distribution, GPU utilization, and cost-per-1k tokens estimate.

[05:12] Raj: When you say KV cache — are you talking about the model's kv cache or some external cache? We have some concerns about cache warming and cold-starts for many short-lived sessions.

[05:25] Jamal: It's the transformer KV cache we leverage for multi-turn chat and prefix caching in the runtime. We also have request-level caching options for embeddings and rerank calls. Cold starts are reduced with warm pools and continuous batching. For short sessions we tune the batch window and we can recommend quantization profiles that reduce latency too.

[06:00] Sofia: Network-wise: private option is appealing because we can keep egress bounded. But we need to know exact networking patterns — does Redwood call back into our infra, or do we route to you?

[06:14] Jamal: For hosted, your requests go out to Redwood endpoints — standard TLS egress. For private VPC, your control plane can be customer-managed and inference can run in your VPC or on-prem, so there's no egress. We support VPC peering, private link equivalents, and on-prem packages with locked-down firewall rules. There is a setup window for private of ~4-6 weeks typically depending on infra approvals.

[06:50] Lena: OK. SOC2 and KMS — what's the level of integration? We need to be able to use our KMS/HSM for key management and full audit logs for who accessed tokens and model history.

[07:05] Jamal: We integrate with common KMS providers and can support customer-managed keys for private deployments. We produce audit logs, and have role-based access controls. For hosted we supply SOC2 report and we can set additional contractual terms for log retention. For enterprise customers we can negotiate retention and export formats.

[07:35] Chris: Pricing question — if we start with hosted for quick wins and then move to dedicated, how do credits or committed capacity work?

[07:46] Maya: You can start on hosted usage-based; we will issue free credits for devs. If you move to dedicated, there is a reserved capacity commitment monthly; we typically credit unused hosted balance against committed contracts in pilot conversions. We'll share the pricing sheet after this call.

[08:15] Raj: Any benchmarking folks we can work with to reproduce our production QPS at cost targets? We want to see a cost per 1k tokens estimate for our specific prompts and average sequence length (~180 tokens).

[08:30] Jamal: Yes — jamal will run an initial perf run and produce a CSV with latency percentiles, token counts, and estimated cost. We often run the benchmark across a few model variants (fp16, int8 quantized) to show tradeoffs.

[09:00] Lena: Are there examples of other customers in our vertical that ran a similar dedicated pilot?

[09:07] Maya: We have a couple med-tech and reg-fin customers, I can pull anonymized case notes. We also have a short reference list if you'd like to speak to someone.

[09:30] Sofia: Operationally we need an SSO integration. Do you support SAML or OIDC?

[09:36] Jamal: Both. SAML/Sso and OIDC are supported for hosted and dedicated. For private you can integrate directly with your IdP.

[09:52] Chris: What's the demo/runbook we can hand to devs to get to first token?

[09:56] Maya: We have a Quickstart repo and SDK examples — typically a step-by-step that gets you to first call in 15-30 minutes if the dev has an API key. With free credits we can make sure keys are pre-provisioned for a small team.

[10:20] Raj: Any caveats about model drift or regression monitoring during rollouts?

[10:28] Jamal: We have quality monitoring tied to prompt sets/evals and regression alerts for model outputs. Rollouts support canary and A/B and automatic fallback to compatible variants. You can also pin a model version for deterministic behavior.

[10:45] Lena: For the pilot we want to test two flows: 1) a hosted quickstart for devs to validate prompt quality and cost, and 2) a dedicated small pool to validate latency at 120 qps. Does that sound like a reasonable split?

[10:58] Maya: That's exactly our recommended approach. We'll provision dev credits and stand up a small dedicated pool for the perf run.

[11:10] Sofia: Firewall and egress checklist — Jamal, can you share a one-page networking guide so our infra team can vet it quickly?

[11:18] Jamal: Yep, we'll attach the networking runbook and private deployment checklist.

[11:30] Chris: What about contract lead times and an NDA — we may need to share sensitive sample docs.

[11:36] Maya: We can send an NDA and standard pilot SOW. Typically pilot paperwork is lightweight; for enterprise SOWs we take about 1-2 weeks once scope is agreed.

[11:50] Raj: One technical nit — sequence length distributions: our average is 180 tokens but we have occasional long docs up to 4k tokens. How does that affect latency/cost?

[12:05] Jamal: Long sequences primarily affect memory and per-token latency. We can select a model variant and kernel optimizations tuned for longer context windows; for very long docs we often recommend chunking + retrieval augmented generation (RAG) to control cost. We'll show empirical numbers in the benchmark.

[12:30] Lena: Great. Anything else on security or compliance?

[12:35] Maya: We'll include SOC2 attestation, ISO if available, and the KMS integration notes in the packet.

[12:45] Chris: Ok let's recap next steps.

[12:50] Maya: Recap: 1) Redwood to provision dev credits and send quickstart repo, 2) Apogee to share redacted sample and QPS profile, 3) Redwood SE to run benchmark and return results, 4) Redwood to send pricing + pilot SOW + NDA.

[13:15] Lena: Sounds good. Can we lock a perf-run slot on Dec 4th?

[13:22] Jamal: I have a slot at 10:00 UTC on Dec 4th; I'll book that after the call.

[13:30] Maya: Perfect, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the packet. Thanks everyone.

[13:38] Raj: Thanks, bye.

End of meeting.
